subject: computer-science
title: Virtual Memory and Paging
welcome_lead: How the OS gives every process its own seemingly infinite memory.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: virtual memory, paging, page tables and swap.
final_note: Virtual memory turns a small RAM into a large illusion.

concepts.def: An abstraction giving each process its own large address space.
A fixed-size block of virtual memory, often 4 KB.
Data structure mapping virtual pages to physical frames.
An access to a page not currently in RAM, triggering OS handling.
Disk space used to hold pages evicted from RAM.
Translation Lookaside Buffer — a cache for page table entries.

walkthroughs.body_html: Virtual memory isolates processes, allows over-commit and supports memory protection. Each process sees its own contiguous space; the MMU translates virtual addresses to physical ones at runtime.
Memory is divided into pages (commonly 4 KB) and matching frames in RAM. The page table maps pages to frames. A miss is a page fault handled by the OS.

Looking up the page table on every access would be slow, so the CPU caches recent translations in the TLB. A TLB hit is nearly free; a miss costs a memory access (or several on multilevel page tables).
